common_name: Sunrise Coneflower (Soft Yellow Big Sky Series Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunrise is part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred for expanded color range.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sunrise bears large, soft lemon-yellow blooms with slightly drooping petals around a coppery-orange cone, part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred to expand the color palette beyond the traditional purple-pink of straight Echinacea purpurea. It blooms over a long summer season and, like other coneflowers, tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Milkshake bears fully double, rounded, pure white pompom blooms with no visible cone or ray petals.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Milkshake produces unusual, fully double, creamy white pompom blooms in which the petals have multiplied into a rounded mass with no distinct cone visible, a striking novelty form quite different from the simple daisy shape of straight-species coneflower. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established, though the fully double flowers are generally less valuable to pollinators than single-flowered coneflowers. Deadhead for continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Butterfly Kisses Coneflower (Dwarf Double Pink Pompom Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Butterfly Kisses is a dwarf double-flowered coneflower well suited to containers and small borders.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Butterfly Kisses bears fragrant, fully double, rose-pink pompom blooms on a compact, dwarf plant considerably shorter than most coneflower cultivars, fitting neatly into containers, small borders, or the front of a bed where taller coneflowers would overwhelm the space. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Summer Sky Coneflower (Pink-and-Orange Bicolor Big Sky Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Summer Sky is part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers, bearing bicolor pink-and-orange blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Summer Sky bears petals that shift from soft pink at the base to warm orange at the tips around a coppery-orange cone, a sunset-toned bicolor effect distinctive among the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred to expand the traditional purple-pink coneflower palette. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches.

common_name: Nicky Phlox (Deep Magenta-Purple Mildew-Resistant Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Nicky bears large, rounded flower heads in deep magenta-purple, a bold, saturated color that holds up well through the heat of summer, blooming over a long stretch from midsummer into early fall with the classic sweet fragrance of tall garden phlox. It shows better than average resistance to powdery mildew compared to older pink and purple cultivars, though full sun and generous spacing still help keep foliage clean. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

common_name: Laura Phlox (Purple-Violet with White Eye Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Laura bears rounded flower heads in rich purple-violet, each petal marked with a small white eye at the center, a crisp two-tone combination that carries the classic sweet fragrance of tall garden phlox through a long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. Like most Phlox paniculata cultivars it benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew, performing best as a shorter-lived perennial in the hottest Gulf South gardens. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

common_name: Shortwood Phlox (Clear Pink High-Performance Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Shortwood is a top-performing pink garden phlox in university trial gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Shortwood bears large, clear pink flower heads on tall, vigorous stems, and has repeatedly ranked among the top-performing tall garden phlox cultivars in university trial gardens for its combination of strong color, mildew resistance, and reliable vigor. It carries the classic sweet fragrance of the species through a long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which typically revert toward magenta.

common_name: Starfire Phlox (Classic Deep Crimson-Red Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Starfire is a classic older cultivar valued for the deepest red color among garden phlox.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Starfire bears rounded flower heads in deep crimson-red, among the richest, darkest reds found in tall garden phlox, opening on dark-tinted stems that add further contrast, and carries the classic sweet fragrance of the species through a midsummer bloom season. Like most older Phlox paniculata cultivars it is more prone to powdery mildew than newer resistant selections, so give it full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

common_name: Katherine Phlox (Lavender-Blue with White Eye Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Katherine bears rounded flower heads in soft lavender-blue, each petal marked with a small white eye, a cool, gentle color that stands apart from the hot pinks and reds typical of most garden phlox, carrying the classic sweet fragrance of the species through a long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. It benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

common_name: Peppermint Twist Phlox (White with Magenta Candy-Stripe Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Peppermint Twist bears distinctive candy-striped petals unlike most solid-colored garden phlox.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Peppermint Twist bears white petals striped down the center with a bright magenta-pink candy stripe, a novelty pattern that stands out sharply from the solid-colored blooms typical of most garden phlox, carrying the classic sweet fragrance of the species. It benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew, and stripe patterning can vary somewhat from flower to flower. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which revert to solid colors.

common_name: Norah Leigh Phlox (Cream-and-Green Variegated Foliage Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Norah Leigh is grown chiefly for its cream-and-green variegated foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Norah Leigh is grown as much for its striking cream-and-green variegated foliage as for its pale lilac flowers, providing season-long interest in the border even before the modest summer bloom appears; the variegation is generally most vivid on younger growth and can fade somewhat as the season progresses. Like most Phlox paniculata cultivars it needs good air circulation and consistent moisture to resist powdery mildew. Remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly, since they grow more vigorously than the variegated stems and can overtake the plant.

common_name: Natasha Phlox (White with Pink-Magenta Stripe Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Natasha bears distinctive candy-striped petals, a separate striped-petal selection from Peppermint Twist.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Natasha bears white petals striped with vivid pink-magenta down the center of each, a separately registered striped-petal cultivar distinct from Peppermint Twist though the pattern reads similarly at a glance, carrying the classic sweet fragrance of tall garden phlox. It benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew, and stripe patterning can vary somewhat from flower to flower. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which revert to solid colors.

common_name: Woods Blue Aster (Compact Mildew-Resistant Blue-Violet New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Woods Blue is a compact, mildew-resistant New York aster selection well suited to smaller borders.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Woods Blue forms a compact, dense mound smothered in small, blue-violet, daisy-form flowers each fall, considerably more resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures larger New York aster cultivars by late summer. Its tidy, low habit suits it to the front of a border or a mass planting where a compact fall-blooming perennial is wanted. Pinch or shear back by one-third in early summer to keep growth bushy and delay bloom slightly, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Woods Pink Aster (Compact Mildew-Resistant Clear Pink New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Woods Pink is a compact, mildew-resistant New York aster selection well suited to smaller borders.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Woods Pink forms a compact, dense mound smothered in small, clear pink, daisy-form flowers each fall, considerably more resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures larger New York aster cultivars by late summer. Its tidy, low habit and soft color suit it to the front of a border or a mass planting where a compact fall-blooming perennial is wanted. Pinch or shear back by one-third in early summer to keep growth bushy and delay bloom slightly, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Monch is a Frikart's aster hybrid noted for an exceptionally long bloom season from summer into fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Monch bears large, lavender-blue, daisy-form flowers with a golden center over a remarkably long season stretching from midsummer well into fall, far longer than most fall-blooming asters, on a bushy, well-branched plant. It is widely regarded among perennial growers as one of the best all-around garden asters for sustained bloom and general reliability. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Snow Flurry Aster (Prostrate Groundcover White Heath Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Snow Flurry is a prostrate, groundcover-form selection of native heath aster.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Snow Flurry hugs the ground in a dense, spreading mat only a few inches tall, smothered each fall in tiny white daisy flowers, an unusual groundcover form of the native heath aster useful for rock gardens, slopes, or the front edge of a sunny border where a low-growing fall bloomer is wanted. It tolerates poor, lean soil and drought well once established, in keeping with its origin as a tough native wildflower. Cut back in late winter to tidy the mat before new growth emerges in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Bluebird is a selection of native smooth aster valued for good mildew resistance and upright habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Bluebird bears abundant blue-violet, daisy-form flowers with a golden center on tall, upright, sturdy stems clothed in smooth, blue-green foliage that stays notably clean and mildew-free compared to many garden asters. As a selection of a widespread North American native, it tolerates a range of soils and needs little care beyond staking in very rich soil where growth may be lush. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.
